title: 22. Interview: Latency

Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why are latency percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9) more useful than averages?
**Answer:** Averages hide outliers, but outliers are exactly what users notice. The mean of [10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 1000] ms is 109ms, suggesting the system is "about 100ms" — but 10% of users see a full second of latency. Percentiles expose the distribution: p50=10ms tells you the typical experience; p99=1000ms tells you the worst 1% experience; p99.9 tells you the worst 0.1%. At scale, even p99 matters: a service handling 1B requests/day has 10M p99 requests daily — that's 10M users who saw a slow response. Percentiles also let you set meaningful SLOs ("p99 < 200ms") and detect regressions ("p99 jumped from 50ms to 300ms after the last deploy"). The pitfall: percentiles require enough samples to be statistically meaningful — p99.9 from 100 samples is noise. Production systems use sliding windows of thousands to millions of samples. Also, percentiles don't compose linearly — the p99 of a service calling 10 backends is not the p99 of any individual backend, due to tail amplification.
**Visual:**
```
[10,10,10,10,10,10,10,10,10,1000] ms
mean = 109 ms      <- misleading
p50  = 10 ms       <- typical user
p99  = 1000 ms     <- 1% see full second
```

### Q2. What is tail-latency amplification, and how do you mitigate it?
**Answer:** Tail-latency amplification occurs when a request depends on multiple backend calls in parallel — the overall latency is the max (slowest) of the calls, so even a small fraction of slow calls dominates the tail. If a single backend has p99=100ms, then for a request that fans out to 10 such backends, P(at least one is slow) = 1 - 0.99^10 = 9.6% — the p99 of the combined request is now ~600ms, 6x the individual p99. At 100 fan-out, P(at least one slow) = 63%, and the p99 of the combined is the worst-case of any backend. Mitigations: (1) Hedged requests — send a second request after a delay (e.g., 20ms) and use whichever returns first; this dramatically cuts p99 because two independent slow calls are unlikely. (2) Bound the fan-out — if the application needs only some of the results, send requests to a subset and add more only if needed. (3) Aggressively cache slow dependencies so they're rarely called. (4) Use deadline propagation so each layer knows the remaining time budget and can short-circuit. (5) Reduce the slow fraction itself — fix GC pauses, lock contention, and hot partitions. Google's "Tail at Scale" paper describes these techniques in depth.
**Visual:**
```
Single call:  p99=100ms
Fan-out 10:   P(slow)=9.6%, p99~600ms
Fan-out 100:  P(slow)=63%,  p99~1000ms

Mitigation - hedged request:
  Send call A at t=0
  If A not returned by t=20ms, send call B
  Use whichever returns first
  -> P(both slow) = 0.01 * 0.01 = 0.0001, p99 drops dramatically
```

### Q3. Explain the latency-vs-throughput trade-off using Little's Law.
**Answer:** Little's Law states `L = λW`, where L is the number of requests in flight, λ is throughput (requests/sec), and W is latency (sec). Rearranged: `λ = L/W` — throughput is bounded by concurrency and latency. The trade-off emerges because latency W is not constant — it grows non-linearly with utilization. At low utilization, W is dominated by service time (the actual work); at high utilization, W is dominated by queueing wait time, which grows as `1/(1-ρ)` where ρ is utilization. At 50% utilization, queueing adds 2x the service time; at 90%, it adds 10x; at 99%, it adds 100x. This is why production systems target 70-80% CPU — beyond that, latency explodes even before throughput peaks. Batching is the classic trade-off lever: batching N requests into one improves throughput by reducing per-request overhead, but adds latency while waiting for the batch to fill. The right batch size depends on workload: latency-sensitive (small batches or single requests) vs throughput-sensitive (large batches). Kafka's linger.ms, database bulk inserts, and HTTP/2 multiplexing all exploit this trade-off.
**Visual:**
```
Utilization   Throughput   Latency
50%           50%          ~2x service time
70%           70%          ~3x service time  <- target
90%           90%          ~10x service time
99%           99%          ~100x service time  <- unusable
```

### Q4. What are the main sources of latency in a distributed system, and how do you mitigate each?
**Answer:** Four main sources: (1) Network latency — speed-of-light round-trip plus router hops. A US-Europe RTT is ~80ms; cross-Pacific ~150ms. Mitigation: CDN edge caching, geographic deployment, Anycast routing. You cannot beat physics; you can only move compute closer to users. (2) Queueing latency — requests waiting for a busy server. Grows non-linearly with utilization. Mitigation: keep servers below 70-80% utilization, use adaptive load shedding, autoscale proactively. (3) Processing latency — CPU time for parsing, computing, serializing. Mitigation: algorithmic improvements, profile-guided optimization, faster languages for hot paths (Rust/C++), reduce serialization (use binary protocols like Protobuf). (4) GC pauses — JVM stop-the-world events, typically 10ms-1s. Mitigation: tune GC (ZGC, Shenandoah for sub-10ms pauses), reduce allocation in hot paths, use off-heap storage for large caches, consider non-JVM languages for latency-critical paths. Each source has a distinct signature in metrics: network is constant per region; queueing grows with load; processing is constant per request; GC is periodic spikes. Diagnose by correlating latency spikes with each source.
**Visual:**
```
Source         Signature              Fix
Network        constant per region    CDN, geographic deploy
Queueing       grows with load        keep <80% util, load shed
Processing     constant per request   optimize algorithms, use fast lang
GC             periodic spikes        ZGC, reduce allocation, off-heap
```

### Q5. What is a latency budget, and how does it cascade through a system?
**Answer:** A latency budget is the maximum end-to-end latency the user will accept, decomposed into per-layer sub-budgets. If the product page must render in 200ms, you might allocate 100ms to the API, 50ms to the database, 30ms to the network, and 20ms to the client render. Each layer's SLO is its sub-budget; exceeding it anywhere breaks the overall SLO. The budget cascades: the API layer knows it has 100ms total, so it allocates 50ms to its primary database call, 30ms to a downstream service, and 20ms for its own processing. If the downstream service exceeds 30ms, the API layer must short-circuit (return cached data or degrade) rather than blow the total budget. Deadline propagation is the implementation: the client passes a deadline (e.g., "must respond by t=200ms"), and each layer subtracts the time it has spent before calling the next layer. This ensures the entire system respects the user-facing SLO rather than each layer optimizing locally. The pitfall: without explicit budgets, each layer adds "just a few ms" and the total balloons; with budgets, you force hard trade-offs and surface design issues early.
**Visual:**
```
User budget: 200ms total
  |
  +-- Network: 30ms
  +-- API layer: 100ms (budget after network)
  |     +-- Auth: 5ms
  |     +-- Downstream call: 50ms (deadline propagated)
  |     +-- Processing: 45ms
  +-- Client render: 50ms

If downstream exceeds 50ms, API short-circuits to fallback.
```

### Q6. Explain the hedged request technique and when to use it.
**Answer:** A hedged request sends a second copy of the request after a delay (e.g., 20ms) if the first hasn't returned, and uses whichever response comes first, canceling the loser. The math: if the slow-fraction is 1%, then P(both copies slow) = 0.0001 — the combined p99 drops from the individual p99 to roughly the individual p95. This is a powerful tool for cutting tail latency in systems with parallel redundancy. Use it when: (1) the downstream is replicated (multiple identical copies serving reads), so the second request can go to a different replica; (2) the workload is read-heavy and idempotent (writes need careful handling to avoid duplication); (3) the tail is caused by transient slowness (GC, queueing, hot partition), not by systematic slowness. Don't use it when: (1) the downstream is single-replica — the second request just doubles load with no benefit; (2) the workload is write-heavy and not idempotent — you risk duplicate writes; (3) the system is already at high utilization — hedging adds load and may worsen the tail. Google uses hedging extensively in its internal infrastructure; Amazon DynamoDB uses a variant called "adaptive hedging" that adjusts the delay based on observed latency. The pitfall: uncontrolled hedging multiplies load — bound the hedge rate.
**Visual:**
```
t=0ms:    send request A to replica 1
t=20ms:   if A not returned, send request B to replica 2
t=?:      use first response, cancel the other

P(A slow) = 1%, P(B slow) = 1%, P(both slow) = 0.01%
p99 of hedged = ~p95 of single
```

### Q7. How does Amazon's 100ms latency finding shape their architecture?
**Answer:** Amazon's finding — that 100ms of additional latency on the product page reduced sales by 1% — is treated as a design constraint that ripples through the entire architecture. (1) CDN edge caching puts product images and static assets within ~10ms of every user globally via CloudFront. (2) DynamoDB was built explicitly to provide single-digit-millisecond p99 latency at any scale, using SSDs, consistent hashing, and B-tree partitioning — relational databases with their lock contention and query planning variability couldn't meet the SLO. (3) The product page is assembled from dozens of microservices in parallel, with strict per-service latency budgets — a service exceeding its budget is called out and is a candidate for caching or replacement. (4) Two-pizza teams own services with explicit latency SLOs, tracked and enforced via dashboards and alarms. (5) Latency is treated as a feature, not a side effect — product managers include latency in feature specs, and engineers design for it from day one. The lesson for other systems: pick a latency target that matches the business cost of slowness, decompose it into budgets, and enforce the budgets through SLOs and architecture. Latency is not a property that emerges by accident; it is the result of disciplined trade-offs.
**Visual:**
```
Amazon product page SLO: 200ms total
  CDN images:        10ms
  API gateway:       10ms
  Product service:   50ms (parallel: catalog, price, reviews, stock)
  Network RTT:       30ms
  Client render:     100ms
  Total:            200ms

Each box is owned by a 2-pizza team with its own SLO.
Exceed budget -> alarm -> post-mortem -> fix.
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your API typically responds in 50ms at p50 but spikes to 2 seconds at p99. How do you diagnose the cause?
**Answer:** The gap between p50 and p99 indicates a tail-latency problem, not a steady-state slowness. Diagnose by correlating the spikes with each potential source. (1) Check GC logs if the service is JVM-based — periodic 2s spikes every few minutes point to Full GC pauses. Fix with ZGC/Shenandoah, larger heap, or reduced allocation. (2) Check CPU utilization at the spike times — if CPU is at 100%, queueing latency is the cause; the fix is autoscaling or load shedding. (3) Check downstream service latencies — if a downstream service has p99=2s, it dominates your p99. Add a circuit breaker and timeout. (4) Check database slow-query logs — a missing index or a lock-contended write can spike to seconds. Add an index or move the write off the hot path. (5) Check network metrics — if there's a spike in retransmits or DNS lookups at the same time, network jitter is the cause. (6) Look at the distribution — are the slow requests correlated with specific data (e.g., large payloads, specific users) or random? Random points to GC or queueing; correlated points to data-specific issues. The diagnostic approach: instrument every layer, capture flame graphs and GC logs, and correlate the p99 spikes with events in each layer. Without per-layer visibility, you're guessing.
**Visual:**
```
p50=50ms, p99=2000ms
  |
  +-- GC pause every 5min?  -> JVM logs
  +-- CPU 100% at spike?    -> autoscale, load shed
  +-- downstream p99 high?  -> circuit breaker, timeout
  +-- DB slow query?        -> add index, fix query
  +-- network retransmits?  -> check NIC, MTU, DNS
```

### Q2. You're building a global e-commerce site. Users in Asia complain the site is slow. Your servers are in us-east. What do you do?
**Answer:** The fundamental problem is network latency — Asia-to-US-East round-trip is 200-300ms, and every page load requires multiple round-trips, so 1-2 seconds of latency is unavoidable from physics alone. Mitigations in priority order: (1) Deploy CDN edge nodes in Asia (CloudFront, Akamai, Cloudflare) to cache static assets — images, CSS, JS — within ~10ms of users. This alone cuts perceived latency dramatically. (2) Deploy read replicas of the product catalog in Asia — most e-commerce traffic is read-heavy (browse, search), and serving reads locally eliminates the cross-Pacific round-trip. (3) For dynamic content, deploy API servers in Asia that call the local read replicas for product data and only call us-east for write operations (checkout, account updates). Writes are less latency-sensitive because the user is already committed to the action. (4) For the checkout flow specifically, consider a multi-region active-active database (DynamoDB Global Tables, Spanner, CockroachDB) so writes can happen locally and replicate async. (5) Use prefetching and HTTP/2 to reduce round-trips — combine API calls, use server push for critical assets. (6) Measure real user monitoring (RUM) — actual user latency in production, not synthetic tests — to verify the improvements. The principle: at global scale, geographic distribution is not optional; it is the only way to beat the speed of light.
**Visual:**
```
Asia user -> CDN edge (Asia)        10ms  (static)
          -> API server (Asia)      20ms  (reads from local replica)
          -> product DB replica     5ms   (Asia)
          -> checkout write         250ms (sync to us-east)
                                     ^
                                     only writes cross Pacific
```

### Q3. Your service's p99 latency jumped from 100ms to 500ms after a deploy. The deploy added a new feature that calls a downstream service. How do you triage?
**Answer:** Triage in order of likelihood and ease of diagnosis. (1) Check the new downstream call's latency distribution — if its p99 is 400ms, it's dominating your p99. Add a timeout (e.g., 100ms) and a circuit breaker, and consider whether the call is on the critical path or can be made async. (2) Check if the new feature added CPU-intensive work — profile the service and compare flame graphs before/after the deploy. (3) Check if the feature changed the request fan-out — if it now calls 10 downstreams in parallel where it used to call 1, tail amplification is multiplying the latency. (4) Check for new GC pressure — if the feature allocates more objects, GC frequency may have increased, spiking p99. (5) Check the database — if the feature adds a query, it may be missing an index or hitting a hot partition. (6) If the feature is async (queues, background work), check if it's stealing CPU from the request path. Immediate mitigation: rollback or feature-flag off the new code. Long-term: ensure every new downstream call has a timeout, circuit breaker, and explicit latency budget; add a latency regression test that fails CI if p99 exceeds the budget. The lesson: latency regressions are typically introduced by new code, and a strict latency SLO enforced in CI catches them before production.
**Visual:**
```
Before:  client -> service (50ms) -> DB (10ms) = 60ms
After:   client -> service (50ms) -> DB (10ms)
                       |
                       +-> new downstream (400ms) <- dominates!
Fix: timeout 100ms + circuit breaker + async off critical path
```

### Q4. Your team's Kafka consumer has p99 processing latency of 5 seconds, but p50 is 50ms. The throughput is fine. What's happening, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** High p99 with low p50 in a Kafka consumer typically means a small fraction of messages take much longer to process, causing head-of-line blocking for the messages behind them. Likely causes: (1) A specific message type triggers expensive processing — e.g., a large message, a message that hits a slow database query, or a message requiring an external API call with no timeout. Profile by logging per-message processing time and finding the slow ones. (2) Lock contention — if multiple consumer threads share a resource (a database connection pool, a cache), occasional contention can spike latency. (3) GC pauses in the JVM consumer. (4) The consumer is processing messages in a single thread per partition, and a slow message blocks the partition. Fixes: (1) Add per-message processing time limits — if processing exceeds N ms, log and skip (or move to a dead-letter topic). (2) Move slow messages to a separate topic with dedicated consumers, so they don't block fast messages. (3) Increase parallelism — more partitions and more consumers — so a slow message on one partition doesn't block others. (4) Add timeouts on all downstream calls from the consumer. (5) Tune GC if JVM pauses are the cause. (6) Consider batch processing for slow operations — accumulate messages and process in a background thread, decoupling consumption from processing. The key insight: in a sequential consumer, one slow message blocks the whole partition, so isolating slow messages is essential.
**Visual:**
```
partition: [fast][fast][fast][SLOW 5s][fast][fast][fast]
                                  ^
                                  blocks everything behind it
Fix:
  - timeout per message (skip or DLQ the slow one)
  - move slow messages to separate topic
  - more partitions + more consumers for parallelism
```

### Q5. You're designing a real-time multiplayer game server. Players complain about "rubber-banding" — their character positions jump backward. Latency is the cause. How do you architect for low latency?
**Answer:** Real-time multiplayer is one of the most latency-sensitive workloads — players notice anything above 50ms, and 150ms is unplayable. Architecture: (1) Geographic deployment — game servers in every major region (NA, EU, Asia, etc.), with players matched to the nearest region by ping. (2) UDP, not TCP — TCP's head-of-line blocking and retransmission add latency; UDP lets you drop stale packets and send only the latest state. (3) Client-side prediction — the client predicts the player's movement locally and reconciles with the server's authoritative state, masking network latency. (4) Server reconciliation — the server sends back authoritative state, and the client rewinds and replays inputs to correct prediction errors. (5) Interest management — the server only sends updates about entities near the player, reducing bandwidth and processing per update. (6) Lag compensation — for hit detection, the server rewinds the world state to what the shooter saw (accounting for their latency) before judging the hit. (7) Tick rate vs frame rate — server tick rate (typically 20-60Hz) is a trade-off between bandwidth and responsiveness; higher tick rate is better but costs more. (8) Anycast or DNS-based routing to direct players to the closest server. The "rubber-banding" specifically indicates either latency spikes (jitter) or prediction/reconciliation bugs; instrument both network jitter and reconciliation error rate. The principle: at this level of latency sensitivity, every millisecond matters and the architecture must be designed around it from day one.
**Visual:**
```
Player (Asia) -> game server (Asia)        ~20ms RTT
                |
                +-- UDP for state updates (drop stale)
                +-- client predicts movement locally
                +-- server reconciles every tick (60Hz)
                +-- lag comp rewinds for hit detection
No cross-region hops for active gameplay.
```

### Q6. Your team wants to add a "frequently bought together" recommendation to the product page. The recommendation service has p99=300ms. The product page SLO is 200ms total. What do you do?
**Answer:** The recommendation service's p99 exceeds the entire page SLO, so calling it synchronously on the critical path is impossible. Options: (1) Move it off the critical path — render the product page first without recommendations, then load recommendations async via a separate AJAX call after page load. The user sees the page immediately and recommendations appear 300ms later; perceived latency is fine. This is the standard pattern for non-critical enrichments. (2) Cache recommendations aggressively — precompute recommendations for popular products in a background job, store in Redis, and serve from cache (p99 ~5ms). Only call the live recommendation service on cache miss, and even then with a short timeout (e.g., 100ms) and a fallback to "no recommendations." (3) Use a shorter timeout with graceful degradation — call the recommendation service with a 100ms timeout; if it doesn't respond, omit the section entirely. Users see no recommendations on slow requests but the page renders fast. (4) Pre-render recommendations at edge — for the top 1000 products, precompute the recommendation HTML and serve via CDN. (5) If recommendations are critical for conversion, lobby to raise the page SLO or move the recommendation service to a faster stack — but this is the last resort. The right answer is usually (1) + (2): async load with aggressive caching. The principle: not every feature belongs on the critical path; rank features by criticality and degrade non-critical ones aggressively.
**Visual:**
```
Page render (critical):  product, price, image, add-to-cart
                          -> 200ms SLO

Recommendations (non-critical):
  Option A: async AJAX after page load
  Option B: cache in Redis (precomputed)
  Option C: timeout 100ms + omit if slow
```

### Q7. You're asked to set latency SLOs for a new API. The business has no specific numbers. How do you decide?
**Answer:** Start from user perception, not from current performance. Research on human perception of latency: under 100ms feels instantaneous; 100-300ms feels fast; 300-1000ms feels responsive but noticeable; 1-3s feels slow; over 3s users abandon. For most user-facing APIs, target p99 < 300ms and p99.9 < 1s. Refine based on workload: (1) For interactive APIs (search, autocomplete, real-time), target p99 < 100ms — users notice any delay. (2) For transactional APIs (checkout, submit form), p99 < 1s is acceptable — users expect a brief wait. (3) For batch/background APIs (report generation, exports), p99 < 30s is fine. (4) For internal/admin APIs, p99 < 5s is usually acceptable. Set the SLO conservatively at first, then iterate based on actual performance and user feedback. Document the SLO and the rationale — "p99 < 300ms because this is on the critical checkout path where Amazon's research shows 100ms = 1% sales loss." Track the SLO with alerts that fire when the error budget is consumed. Re-evaluate quarterly: if you're consistently under the SLO with budget to spare, you can either tighten it (better user experience) or relax it (cheaper infrastructure). If you're consistently blowing it, invest in performance or re-architect. The pitfall: setting SLOs based on "what we currently achieve" rather than "what users need" locks in mediocrity. Always start from the user.
**Visual:**
```
User perception:
  <100ms: instant       <- interactive APIs (search, autocomplete)
  <300ms: fast          <- user-facing read APIs (product page)
  <1s:   responsive     <- transactional APIs (checkout)
  <3s:   slow           <- background, admin
  >3s:   abandon        <- avoid

Set SLO, track, alert on budget exhaustion, iterate quarterly.
```
